text: TET-56 f3: tetel bounds its own grep return

This memo designs one change: `look --grep` decides for itself how much of a search result it returns to the author, and says in the search label what it withheld. Everything below was observed against a single pinned worktree state, so a reader can re-run any of it.
## Where the bound goes

`look_grep` already does the two jobs separately. It runs grep once, then builds `printed` — the string handed back to the author, which today is grep's stdout verbatim followed by a parenthesised exclusion note — and, independently, the pending entries: one `Search` record carrying the root, the pattern and a matched-file count, and one `GrepMatch` record per matched file carrying that file's matched lines. The two are derived from the same stdout but neither reads the other. That is what makes f3 cheap and what keeps it inside the ticket's scope: a bound imposed while assembling `printed` cannot reach the buffer, so the extent, the pin and the snapshot stay exactly what they are today.
## What the label records

The ticket's phrase "in the search label" is not a stylistic preference; it is the only place that works. A memo's Facts table renders the Extent column as the observation labels joined with `; `, and captured output is deliberately excluded from the document — it is unbounded and lives in the snapshot. So whatever the bound writes into the label is the whole of what a later reader sees about the truncation; anything recorded only in the captured output, or only in the string returned at the time, is invisible in the artefact the design exists to make honest.

Two things follow about the unit, and they point in different directions. The constraint is a byte budget, and bytes are not predictable from lines: on this HEAD a single grep output line reaches 1090 bytes, so a bound of "the first 450 lines" would have let a return through at several hundred kilobytes while still calling itself bounded. But bytes are the wrong thing to cut on, because grep's unit is the line `<file>:<lineno>:<text>` — the same unit `look_grep` splits on to build its per-file records — and a return severed mid-line hands the author a fragment that is not a match. So the rule is: accumulate whole lines, and stop before the first line that would carry the total past the byte budget.
## What the bound is, and where it comes from

There is no honest way to derive the number. The MCP `look` handler receives a workspace, a path, an optional line range and an optional pattern, and hands back `printed` without measuring it; no field anywhere in that call carries a caller's result cap, so tetel cannot learn one at run time. The number is therefore a person's choice, and this crate has already decided how it treats those. `describe_buffer` declined to invent a staleness threshold because "a number chosen here would be arbitrary", and made the underlying fact visible instead. The same shape applies: the constant is a documented judgement, and nothing load-bearing rests on its exact value — what the design guarantees is that whatever was withheld is named. Set it low enough that a caller's cap is not reached first, and if a later caller is stricter, the failure mode is a silent cut returning, which is the very thing being fixed. That is an argument for choosing conservatively, not for pretending the choice was measured.

why: The original paragraph ended with a recommendation ("set it low enough...") that no cited claim carried; the recommendation now lives in C8 and gets its own paragraph, and this one is cut back to what C6 and C7 state.

text: The value proposed is 32 KiB — 32768 bytes — and it is proposed as a judgement, which is the whole of its justification. The single constraint it has to satisfy is that it sit strictly below the caller's cap, because a bound above that cap is not a bound at all: the caller cuts first and invisibly, which is the defect. Since tetel cannot see the cap, the only available discipline is to choose well under any plausible one. What can be stated exactly is its effect on the censuses measured here: seven of the nine return bounded, and `target` and `label` still return whole. A reader who disagrees with 32768 is disagreeing with a judgement, not correcting a measurement, and the design does not change if they win.

This is also the answer to what happens to the other `look` paths, and it is a firm no rather than a deferral. `look_path` computes a single value `shown`, pushes it into the returned string and moves the same value into the pending entry's `output`. There is no separation to exploit: bounding the return there would bound the capture, and changing what is captured is out of scope by construction. So `look --grep` is bounded and `look <path>` is not, and the asymmetry is a fact about the code's shape rather than an omission. It is worth adding that the two paths differ in intent as well — a `--lines A:B` return is already the size the author asked for.

`look --lines` also supplies the precedent for how a shortfall should be spelled. Ask for lines 400 to 900 of a 600-line file and the label reads `lines 400-600`: it records what was delivered, not what was requested. Ask for a range wholly past the end and the label says so explicitly, on the stated principle that a bounded negative must leave a trace. Recording in the label the difference between what was asked for and what came back is therefore already how this module behaves; f3 extends it from a range the author chose to a bound tetel chose.
## The change, and how far it reaches

One function changes. A census of the whole worktree for `look_grep` finds it in two source files: the definition and a single call site in `dispatch`, with the other three occurrences doc comments referring to it. Both the bound and the label are assembled inside the function, and its signature does not change, so nothing calling it needs to be touched — not `dispatch`, not the CLI, not the MCP handler.
## What the census refusal still guarantees

TET-28's refusal is untouched, and its wording needs no amendment. It fires on `ExtentEntry::censuses`, which reads the search's existence and its root out of an extent that is immutable once minted and that a bound on `printed` never reaches. More to the point, the refusal already tells the truth about its own scope: it "is about the search's existence and where it was rooted, never about what it found". A design that bounds what the author is shown does not make that sentence any less accurate — it was never a claim about what the author read.

Carrying that mechanism across brings its two preconditions with it. The donor states that a shortfall is not an error, and the same must hold here: hitting the bound returns a successful outcome with a bounded body, not a refusal. That is both the crate's habit and, in this function, unavoidable — the pending entries are written from the full stdout, so a refusal at that point would be throwing away a capture that has already happened. The donor also states that its key is the resolved path regardless of the range requested, which is what keeps two differently-sized reads of one file overlapping. That holds at the destination too: the `Search` entry is keyed by its root and each match entry by its file, both from paths alone, so a bounded search and an unbounded one of the same root overlap exactly as two unbounded ones would.
## Whether the truncation has to be visible anywhere else

It does, in exactly one further place, and the shape is already settled by TET-46. `check`'s standing non-coverage list gains a line. That list already distinguishes a withholding tetel chose — its own output, skipped during traversal — from things it merely suffers, like the symlinked directories and binary files the platform's grep never visits; the comment beside them insists a deliberate exclusion earns its own line rather than being folded into a sentence about platform accidents. A bound tetel applies to its own return is deliberate, so it gets its own line. And what that line says is a gap nothing can close: the extent records the whole search, and nothing anywhere establishes that the author read all of it. `scope.rs` already registers that limit as permanently out of reach, so the entry is not an admission of a new weakness but the naming of an old one that had been invisible.

The division of labour between the two is also TET-46's, and it answers the "of what unit" question from the other end. Every string in the non-coverage list is static and none is per-search, which is why the exclusion set a particular search was given is written into that search's own label instead. The bound follows the same split: the list carries the general statement that a census's return to its author is bounded, and the label carries the numbers for this search. Neither place needs the other's job, and neither can do it.

The label the design proposes therefore reads, for the `check` census measured above: `search: <root> (grep: check) — 71 files matched — showed 231 of 883 matching lines (32768-byte bound) — <exclusion note>`. The unit is matching lines because that is what grep emits and what `look_grep` itself splits on; converting to bytes in the label would report the budget rather than the census. The file count in front of it needs no change, since it is computed from the full stdout and stays true however little was shown — which is worth noticing, because it means even a heavily bounded return still tells the author truthfully how many files matched. And a search that fits gains no segment at all: absence means whole, the same convention by which `look --lines` annotates a range only when it had to clamp one.
## What an author does when they hit the bound

Nothing new, and the honest form of that answer matters more than a paging flag would. The obvious remedies are closed for the case that motivated the ticket: a census is one search of the whole worktree for the symbol itself, so narrowing the root or trimming the pattern does not yield a smaller census, it yields something that is not a census, and `look --grep` has no other parameter to turn. What an author can do is search a subdirectory as an additional observation standing beside the census rather than replacing it, and — outside the return path entirely — reach the per-file match records, which hold every matched line and ship whole into the snapshot. So the design's claim is narrow and should be read narrowly: it does not give the author back what was withheld; it stops the withholding from being secret.

One objection deserves answering here rather than later, because it is the one the label invites: this crate does not store derived values, it stores events. But that rule is stated as a reason to recompute what a re-run can obtain from the shipped ledger, and the shown-count is not obtainable that way. The `Search` entry carries no output, and the per-file entries record what was captured rather than how much of it was handed back, so once the call returns there is nothing left from which "the author saw 231 of these lines" could be reconstructed. It is an event, it is unrecoverable, and writing it down is the only way it survives.

text: The author is the other audience, and the label does not reach them in time. `look` hands back `printed` and nothing else, on the CLI and over MCP alike; the label first becomes visible one act later, in the `fact` result, by which point the note asserting over that observation has already been supplied as a parameter of the same call. An author who read a bounded return and then wrote "this is every call site" would have committed the assertion before tetel told them anything had been cut — the design's own defect, reappearing on the surface it exists to fix. So the shortfall is written into `printed` as well: one `push_str` at the end of a bounded return, carrying the same numbers the label carries. The crate already has a spelling for this half. `refuse_incomplete` shortens an undischarged premise to its first line for a refusal message and marks it with a trailing ` …`, applied when and only when something was actually removed. f3 keeps both of those properties — cut on a line boundary, mark only when the bound bit — and adds the one thing that spelling does not carry: how much was withheld. An ellipsis tells an author that something was cut; it does not tell them whether they are missing two lines or eight hundred, and for someone deciding whether to look again that difference is the whole of the information.

Where an asymmetry does survive is inside `look_path`, and it is about what a shortfall means rather than about whether the bound applies. Under `--lines A:B` the author named a range, and the label already records that range as delivered — clamped to the file's length, or an explicit "nothing in range" — so the shortfall it reports is one the author asked for. A bound biting on top of that is a second shortfall, chosen by tetel rather than by them, and it is recorded beside the first rather than in place of it. Under a plain `look <path>` there is no author-named range at all: the bound is the only shortfall there is, and naming it is the only thing standing between the author and a cut they would never learn about. Both are spelled the same way — accumulate whole lines, stop before the byte budget, name what was withheld in the label and in the returned text — and neither is an error.

The numerals are there to show the shape; every one of them is computed at run time and will drift as the repository does, and nothing in the design turns on them. On this HEAD that census is 883 matching lines across 70 files — 70 being the distinct filenames among those matching lines, which is what the file count is computed from. An earlier draft said 71, from counting distinct filenames over the whole return, in which the trailing exclusion note contributes a spurious extra one. The unit is matching lines because that is what grep emits and what `look_grep` itself splits on; converting to bytes in the label would report the budget rather than the census. The file count in front of it needs no change, since it is computed from the full stdout and stays true however little was shown — which is worth noticing, because it means even a heavily bounded return still tells the author truthfully how many files matched. And a search that fits gains no segment at all: absence means whole, the same convention by which `look --lines` annotates a range only when it had to clamp one.
why: Review against C17 showed the paragraph editorialising past its claim — "the same error in miniature that the whole design is about" is an interpretation C17 does not carry. Replaced with the plain cause of the miscount, which C17 does carry.

text: `look_grep` already does the two jobs separately. It runs grep once, then builds `printed` — the string handed back to the author, which today is grep's stdout verbatim followed by a parenthesised exclusion note — and, independently, the pending entries: one `Search` record carrying the root, the pattern and a matched-file count, and one `GrepMatch` record per matched file carrying that file's matched lines. The two are derived from the same stdout but neither reads the other, and that separation is what the bound rests on: out of a bounded call, every entry's captured output, its key and its world-tree markers come back byte-identical to what they are today, so two observations of one root still overlap and a later reader still re-reads the same bytes. What does not stay identical is the extent, the pin and the fact that ships. `facts::mint` copies each entry's label straight into the extent and hashes label, world markers and output into the pin, and this design writes a shortfall segment into the label — so wherever the bound bites, all three differ from what they would otherwise have been. That is the point and not a cost. It is the same property the exclusion note was given when TET-46 chose to list the skipped memo paths rather than count them, so that two searches withholding different things could not fingerprint alike; a bounded search and a whole one should not fingerprint alike either. What makes f3 cheap, and what keeps it inside the ticket's scope, is narrower than "nothing changes": no new record, no second pass over the buffer, nothing read back out of the entries, no signature touched. One number is computed while `printed` is being assembled, and the label is built from that number. The direction matters to whoever implements this — bound first, label from the bound. An implementer who bounds `printed` and leaves the label alone has rebuilt the silent cut this memo exists to remove.
why: C2 was qualified: the paragraph spent the unqualified form, saying extent, pin and snapshot stay exactly what they are today, which is false on any observation where the bound bites because the label goes into both. Restated to say what the separation actually preserves and to give an implementer the direction of the dataflow.

text: It does, in one place beyond the two the design has already settled — the label and the return itself — and the shape of that place is settled by TET-46. `check`'s standing non-coverage list gains a line. That list already distinguishes a withholding tetel chose — its own output, skipped during traversal — from things it merely suffers, like the symlinked directories and binary files the platform's grep never visits; the comment beside them insists a deliberate exclusion earns its own line rather than being folded into a sentence about platform accidents. A bound tetel applies to its own return is deliberate, so it gets its own line. What that line says has to be written about `look` and not about a census, because the plain path read is inside the bound too and it is a different act: no root, no pattern, no exclusion set, and no filtering of any kind. A line phrased around what a search returns would leave every bounded file read with no standing statement anywhere, on the one surface this design nominates for the general case. So the entry states the general form — what `look` returned to its author is bounded; a fact's extent records the whole of what was observed, and nothing establishes that the author was shown all of it. `scope.rs` already registers that second half as permanently out of reach, so the entry is not an admission of a new weakness but the naming of an old one that had been invisible.
why: C15 was qualified: the line as stated is census-shaped, and the design now bounds the plain path read too, which has no search, no root and no exclusions — followed literally the entry would cover look_grep only.

text: The division of labour between the two is also TET-46's, and it answers the "of what unit" question from the other end. Every string in the non-coverage list is static and none is per-search, which is why the exclusion set a particular search was given is written into that search's own label instead. The bound follows the same split, across both bounded paths: the list carries the general statement that what `look` returns to its author is bounded, and each observation's own label carries the numbers for that observation — the search record's label for a search, the path record's for a file read. Neither place needs the other's job, and neither can do it.
why: Follows C16's narrowing from per-search to per-observation, which C15's qualification reached: the numbers now also go into a path label, where there is no search.

text: One objection deserves answering here rather than later, because it is the one the label invites: this crate does not store derived values, it stores events. That rule is stated as a reason to recompute what a re-run can obtain from the shipped ledger, and for the search label the shown-count is not obtainable that way — the `Search` entry carries no output, and the per-file entries record what was captured rather than how much of it was handed back, keyed by filename into a map that does not preserve the order the bound consumed. For the path label the same argument does not work, and it should not be offered there: that entry's output is the whole of the selected text and `facts.jsonl` ships in the snapshot, so replaying the rule over stored bytes would reproduce the number. Two other things carry it instead. The label records what one run showed under the budget that run applied, and the budget is a judgement open to revision, so a later replay answers what today's build would show rather than what this author was shown. And the audience differs: the doctrine's case is `check` recomputing a report from a ledger it holds, whereas a label is read by someone holding the memo, whose Facts table renders labels and no captured output at all — there is nothing in front of them to recompute from. That an observation record may carry a measurement beside its bytes is not novel either; the extent already stores the captured output's length.
why: C19 was qualified: every reason the paragraph gave is grep-shaped, and the path label the design also writes the number into sits on an entry whose complete output ships in the snapshot, where the number is replayable. The two paths are now argued separately.

text: Where an asymmetry does survive is inside `look_path`, and it is about what a shortfall means rather than about whether the bound applies. Under `--lines A:B` the author named a range, and the label already records that range as delivered — clamped to the file's length, or an explicit "nothing in range" — so the shortfall it reports is one the author asked for. A bound biting on top of that is a second shortfall, chosen by tetel rather than by them, and it is recorded beside the first rather than in place of it. Under a plain `look <path>` there is no author-named range at all: the bound is the only shortfall there is, and naming it is the only thing standing between the author and a cut they would never learn about. The spelling is the grep case's, on both surfaces: the label reads `<path> — showed N of M lines (32768-byte bound)`, or `<path> lines {a}-{end} — showed N of M lines (32768-byte bound)` where a range was asked for, with M the line count of what was selected before the bound; the returned text ends with the same segment. The release rule is the grep case's too, floor included — whole lines while a whole line fits, and where none does the first line cut at a character boundary at or below the budget, which the label spells `<path> — showed 0 of M lines; first line cut mid-line at B of L bytes (32768-byte bound)`. This is the path where the floor earns itself, since every file whose first line overruns the budget is read through it. A read that fits gains no segment in either place, and neither case is an error.
why: C20 restated the unfloored release rule that C18's refutation broke, and the plain path read is where the refutation's construction lands; the paragraph now carries the floored rule and its label spelling.

text: Almost nothing new, and the honest form of that answer matters more than a paging flag would. The obvious remedies are closed for the case that motivated the ticket: a census is one search of the whole worktree for the symbol itself, so narrowing the root or trimming the pattern does not yield a smaller census, it yields something that is not a census, and `look --grep` has no other parameter to turn. What an author can do is search a subdirectory as an additional observation standing beside the census rather than replacing it, and — outside the return path entirely — reach the per-file match records, which hold every matched line and ship whole into the snapshot. So the design's claim is narrow and should be read narrowly: it does not give the author back what was withheld; it stops the withholding from being secret, on the surface they read at the time and in the memo afterwards. The bounded plain `look <path>` is the easier case: `--lines A:B` is already a first-class parameter of the same verb, so an author who wants a further whole line of the file asks for it, and each such read keys on the resolved path and therefore overlaps the first. One residue survives even that, and the memo would rather name it than paper it over. A single line longer than the budget is never returned whole by any call: every range containing it yields the same floored fragment, and there is no argument to `look` that reaches the rest. Those bytes are recoverable only where the grep case's are — in the fact's captured output, which for a file read is the complete selected text and ships in the snapshot beside the memo.
why: C18 was refuted: --lines does not reach a line that is itself over budget, and under the unfloored rule such a read returned nothing at all. The paragraph now states what the floor recovers and names the residue that stays unreadable rather than asserting a remedy that does not exist.

text: Two things follow about the unit, and they point in different directions. The constraint is a byte budget, and bytes are not predictable from lines: on this HEAD a single grep output line reaches 1090 bytes, so a bound of "the first 450 lines" would have let a return through at several hundred kilobytes while still calling itself bounded. But bytes are the wrong thing to cut on, because grep's unit is the line `<file>:<lineno>:<text>` — the same unit `look_grep` splits on to build its per-file records — and a return severed mid-line hands the author a fragment that is not a match. So the first half of the rule is: accumulate whole lines, and stop before the first line that would carry the total past the byte budget. There has to be a second half, for a reason the next paragraph takes up.
why: C5 now carries a floor, and this paragraph stated the whole-lines rule as if it were the complete rule; it is marked as the first half so the paragraph does not assert more than its claim carries.

text: On its own that rule has a hole, and not a hypothetical one. If the first line it considers is by itself over budget, no whole line fits, and the return is a header with nothing under it and a label truthfully reporting that nothing was shown. Four tracked files in this repository are exactly that shape — all of them tetel's own snapshot ledgers, the longest carrying a single line of 905745 bytes — and nothing keeps them out of reach, since a plain `look` refuses only a missing path and a directory and filters nothing at all. In that case a whole-lines-only rule is worse than the silent truncation it replaces: the caller's cut at least hands the author the first tens of kilobytes of that line, and this design would hand them none of it. So the rule takes a floor. Where no whole line fits, the return carries the first line cut at the largest character boundary at or below the budget, and both surfaces say it was cut mid-line rather than reporting a line count alone. That gives up something real, and the memo should name it rather than let it pass: a floored return can hand the author a fragment that is not a whole match record, which is the thing the line-boundary rule was chosen to prevent. What survives the cut is the prefix — a cut grep line still begins `<file>:<lineno>:`, so the fragment still says which match it came from — and the whole line is still in the per-file record that ships. Against an empty body that is the better trade, and a bounded return is now never empty when what it bounded was not. None of this makes the design return *more* than the caller's truncation would; at 32768 bytes it deliberately returns less, since the budget's one constraint is to sit below a cap tetel cannot observe. What the floor restores is the promise the design actually makes, which was never to return more but to leave nothing withheld without saying so. The cut itself has to be spelled out rather than borrowed: nothing in `src` cuts a string at a byte budget today, and these long lines carry multi-byte characters, so the offset is snapped down to a character boundary instead of being taken raw.

One boundary question has to be settled before the label can be specified, because the label reports a number and the number needs a referent: what exactly is being measured. `printed` is not simply grep's output. The parenthesised exclusion note is pushed onto the end of it as a separate segment, on the matching and the no-match branch alike, so a budget applied to the assembled string would eat that note first — it is last. That would be precisely backwards. TET-46 put the note into the return because silence about an exclusion is ambiguous between nothing having been hidden and nobody having said so, and the return that most needs to name what it withheld is the one already withholding the most. So the budget applies to the stdout portion alone. The note sits outside it, and so does the shortfall segment, which means a bounded return runs a little past the budget by the length of what it says about itself. The number in the label and in the segment measures the content, not the string.

The floor is worth spelling out on this path because this is where it is reachable, but it is reached by a range and not by a plain read, and the memo would rather say so than let an implementer discover it from a failing test. The four tracked ledgers that carry an over-budget line all carry it in the middle: at line 11 and line 15 of 20, at line 15 of 21, at line 2 of 11, at line 2 of 10. The floor fires when and only when the first line of the selection is itself over budget, which on these four files means exactly five ranges — `--lines 11:B` and `--lines 15:B` on the first, `--lines 15:B` on the second, `--lines 2:B` on each of the others. A regression test for the floor has to be written on one of those, or on a fixture whose first line exceeds the budget; a test that expects a floored return from a plain read of one of these paths asserts something false.

The paragraph now names the ranged reads that do reach it, so an implementer builds the regression test on a read that floors. The same verdict noted that the paragraph specified the label numbers without settling what the budget measures over on this path, which the memo declares must be settled first; that settlement is now written here.

Its selection and its label are produced together by one `match` on the requested range, and all three arms of that `match` finish the label before the string the bound applies to has been created at all; the label is then handed to the pending entry untouched. An implementer who bounds the returned string where the selection is pushed into it, and leaves that `match` alone, has written a cut return with a label that says nothing about the cut — the exact defect this memo exists to remove, on the path it was added to last. So the `match` yields the base label only, and the shortfall segment is appended to it after the release rule has run over the selected text.
why: C20 was qualified: it specified spelling, referent and floor for `look_path` but not the order of the edit, and the memo's only ordering instruction is scoped to `look_grep` — where the code order already makes it natural. On `look_path` the label is fixed before `printed` exists, so the natural edit reintroduces the silent cut. Carrying the instruction into this paragraph.

text: On its own that rule has a hole, and not a hypothetical one — but it is a hole about the first line of a selection, not about a file. If the first line the rule considers is by itself over budget, no whole line fits, and the return is a header with nothing under it and a label truthfully reporting that nothing was shown. A file that merely holds a long line somewhere does not produce that state: the accumulation stops before the long line and hands back whatever whole lines preceded it. Four tracked files in this repository do hold such a line — all of them tetel's own snapshot ledgers, the longest carrying a single line of 905745 bytes — and nothing keeps them out of reach, since a plain `look` refuses only a missing path and a directory and filters nothing at all. In none of the four, though, is that line the first: the over-budget lines sit at positions 11 and 15 of 20, 15 of 21, 2 of 11 and 2 of 10, so a read that begins at line 1 hands back 5, 2, 1 and 1 whole lines rather than nothing at all. What reaches the empty state is a selection that begins on such a line, and `--lines` supplies it directly — `--lines 15:20` on the longest of the four, `--lines 2:11` on another. There the whole-lines-only rule is strictly worse than the silent truncation it exists to replace: a cap that cuts a long line short still hands the author a prefix of it, and this rule hands them none of it. So the rule takes a floor. Where no whole line fits, the return carries the first line cut at the largest character boundary at or below the budget, and both surfaces say it was cut mid-line rather than reporting a line count alone. That gives up something real, and the memo should name it rather than let it pass: a floored return can hand the author a fragment that is not a whole match record, which is the thing the line-boundary rule was chosen to prevent. What survives the cut is the prefix — a cut grep line still begins `<file>:<lineno>:`, so the fragment still says which match it came from — and the whole line is still in the per-file record that ships. Against an empty body that is the better trade, and a bounded return is now never empty when what it bounded was not. In content the design deliberately returns far less than an unbounded caller would, since the budget's one constraint is to sit below a cap tetel cannot observe; in string length it can run a little past its own budget, because the shortfall segment is text a whole return would not have carried and, like the exclusion note, sits outside the measure. What the floor restores is the promise the design actually makes, which was never to return more but to leave nothing withheld without saying so. The cut itself has to be spelled out rather than borrowed: nothing in `src` cuts a string at a byte budget today, and these long lines carry multi-byte characters, so the offset is snapped down to a character boundary instead of being taken raw.
why: The sentence "None of this makes the design return more than an unbounded caller would" is false in a small window: a bounded return carries a shortfall segment an unbounded one does not, and C22 already settles that the segment sits outside the budget. Correcting the sentence to say what the cited claims say, and citing C22, which is where the exceeding comes from.
